opus-5.5.text:
I think the classical approach has a lot going for it, and I don't want to caricature it. If you can write down an accurate model of your system, the dynamics, the contacts, the environment, then control theory gives you beautiful tools. You can reason about stability, optimality, all of that. For things like airplanes or industrial arms in a structured factory, that has worked extremely well.

The problem comes when you go into the real world, especially with legged robots or manipulation. The world is messy. Think of a quadruped walking on sand, on grass, on a slippery slope, or carrying a payload it didn't expect. The terrain properties, the friction, the softness, the wear on the motors: none of these are known in advance, and they're very hard to model accurately. Contact dynamics in particular are notoriously difficult. So the engineer ends up writing an increasingly complicated model, adding special cases, hand-tuning parameters, and it becomes brittle. It works beautifully in the conditions you designed for and then fails when something is slightly different.

The learning-based approach shifts the burden. Instead of me, the human, having to anticipate every situation and write down the equations, I let the system experience a huge variety of situations, typically in simulation, where I can randomize the terrain, the masses, the frictions, the motor strengths, and learn a policy that works across all of them. What's important, and what we emphasized in our work on rapid motor adaptation, is that the robot also learns to adapt online. It infers from its own recent history of states and actions what kind of environment it's in, an implicit estimate of these extrinsic parameters, and adjusts its behavior within a fraction of a second. That's much closer to what animals and humans do. A child doesn't solve Newton's equations to walk on a beach; they feel it out and adapt.

I'd also make a broader point. In computer vision we went through exactly this transition. People used to handcraft features, edge detectors, SIFT and so on, and the lesson of the last decade was that learned representations, given enough data, outperform what we design by hand. I think robotics is going through a similar transition, with one twist: in robotics, data is expensive, which is why simulation and sim-to-real transfer are so central.

That said, I don't see it as pure learning versus pure classical. The structure from classical control, knowing what the right inputs and outputs are, what the right abstractions are, is often very useful in designing the learning problem. The point is that the final controller doesn't need to be derived by hand; it can be learned, and it's far more robust as a result.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that the classical approach is actually very good when you can do it. If you have a robot arm bolted to a factory floor, you know its mass, its inertia, the geometry of the environment, and you can write down the dynamics and design a controller that works beautifully. That's a real engineering achievement and we shouldn't dismiss it.

The trouble comes when you leave that controlled setting. Think about a legged robot walking outdoors. The ground might be grass, gravel, mud, a slippery patch of ice. The contact dynamics are discontinuous, hard to model, and they change from step to step. The classical approach says: let's model all of that. But you can't. The model is always going to be wrong in ways that matter, and then you spend an enormous amount of human effort tuning things by hand for each new situation.

Learning flips this around. Instead of the engineer having to anticipate every condition, the robot gets experience, in simulation or in the real world, and it adapts its behavior to what actually happens. In the legged locomotion work we did, the policy essentially learns to infer, from how its own body is responding, what kind of terrain it's on, and adjusts. No human wrote down a model of mud.

So I'd put it this way. Classical control gives you precision and guarantees in a world you fully understand. Learning gives you robustness and adaptability in a world you don't. And the real world, frankly, is mostly the second kind. The other thing I'd add is that learning handles perception and control together. In the classical pipeline you have perception on one side producing a state estimate, and control on the other side consuming it, and the interface between them is a bottleneck. With learning you can go more directly from pixels or proprioception to action, and that turns out to be a very big deal.

astra-6.text:
The advantage is that you don’t have to write down an accurate model of everything the robot will encounter. In the classical approach, you specify the dynamics and then design a controller for those dynamics. That works very well when the system is understood and the assumptions are appropriate.

But think about picking up an unfamiliar object. You may not know its mass, its friction, or exactly how the contact with your fingers will behave. Writing down equations that capture all of that is difficult. Learning gives you a way to use experience to handle those uncertainties and improve the behavior.

I wouldn’t frame this as abandoning control theory. We should use the structure that we understand. The opportunity is to learn the parts that are hard to model, and to learn how to act when the model is incomplete.

sol-6.1.text:
The classical approach is to write down a model of the system and then design a controller for that model. When the model is accurate, that works very well. But consider a robot hand manipulating an object. There are contacts, friction, slipping—all sorts of things that are difficult to model accurately. And the moment you pick up a different object, some of those properties change.

The advantage of learning is that the robot can use experience to discover how to act without our having to specify every detail of that interaction. Think about how we learn to pick things up. We don’t first estimate a coefficient of friction and solve a set of equations. We acquire a skill through practice.

That doesn’t mean we should throw away physics or control theory. Those give us useful structure. Learning lets us handle the parts where our models are incomplete, and adapt from experience.

r002.rationale: It says some interaction properties are difficult to model accurately, but does not identify unknown parameters as an obstacle to applying otherwise correct physical equations.

r003.rationale: It mentions properties changing when the robot picks up a different object, not physical parameters changing with terrain.

r005.rationale: It says learning can discover how to act through experience, but does not state that learning simultaneously identifies the system and learns a control law.
